title: Trust in Science Is Falling, Global Survey Finds
paragraphs: During the COVID-19 pandemic, people around the world placed a great deal of trust in science. However, according to a major new global survey, that trust has since fallen to below the levels seen before the pandemic.

The survey, called the Wellcome Global Monitor 2026, was carried out for Wellcome, a large health research charity based in the UK. It was based on interviews with more than 140,000 people in 140 countries, and the results were launched at the World Health Summit in Berlin.

According to the survey, 72% of people said they trusted science "some" or "a lot" in 2025. This was down from 80% in 2020, during the pandemic, and also lower than the 77% recorded in 2018. At the same time, the share of people who said they did not trust science much or at all rose from 13% to 19%.

Trust in scientists has also fallen. In 2018, 34% of people said they trusted scientists "a lot." This figure rose to 43% in 2020, but fell to 32% in 2025. Although scientists are still among the most trusted groups, ranking below doctors and nurses but above journalists and governments, their decline since 2018 was the largest of any group measured.

The survey found that trust in science is closely linked to people's economic situation. Only 20% of people who found it difficult to live on their income said they trusted science "a lot," compared with 39% of people who were living comfortably. This gap has grown since 2018, because trust fell most among people struggling financially. In addition, people who had less trust in their government and national institutions were less likely to trust science.
The situation varies around the world. For example, in sub-Saharan Africa, only 21% of people said they trusted science "a lot," down from 28% in 2018.
According to John-Arne Røttingen, the head of Wellcome, public trust determines whether scientific advances can make a meaningful difference in people's lives.
